title: U-NeXt: General-purpose event detection for neonatal EEG
authors: Robert Hogan; Sean R. Mathieson; Aurel Luca; Soraia Ventura; Sean Griffin; Geraldine B. Boylan; John M. O'Toole
abstract: We developed U-NeXt, a general framework for neonatal electroencephalography (EEG) event detection based on semantic segmentation. Its convolutional encoder-decoder directly segments individual channels using long input segments to preserve temporal context. A shared architecture and training framework were developed using low-voltage interval, artefact, and seizure datasets containing 51, 98, and 278 neonates, respectively, comprising over 11,000 hours of EEG and 82,000 annotated events. Performance was compared with task-specific ConvNeXt classifiers. For seizure detection, we also evaluated U-NeXt+, trained on an expanded dataset. Both U-NeXt variants and the ConvNeXt baseline were evaluated on two independent held-out seizure datasets, Helsinki and Cork, comprising 130 neonates, with recordings annotated by three experts. U-NeXt improved detection across all three event types, with particular gains in sensitivity for short events. U-NeXt+ achieved Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.862 and 0.891 on Helsinki and Cork, respectively, and improved hourly seizure burden correlations by 30-40% relative to ConvNeXt. U-NeXt+ met the criterion for expert-level performance on both datasets (p < 0.001). In separate computational benchmarks, U-NeXt reduced batch inference time relative to ConvNeXt by 254-fold on a central processing unit and 200-fold on a graphics processing unit. A common segmentation framework improves detection across diverse neonatal EEG event types while substantially reducing inference time. Accurate seizure burden estimates and performance comparable to expert reviewers support its potential use in continuous monitoring and clinical decision support.

title: Quantum-Classical Link Prediction on Dark Web Hyperlink Graphs
authors: Vojtěch Novák; Radovan Rečka; Ondřej Knebl; Aktham Youssef; Ivan Zelinka
abstract: We analyze HTML content and hyperlinks from an offline Tor crawl containing 383 onion hosts and 2,067 directed cross-host links. The study combines semantic analysis with degree-controlled quantum--classical link prediction. Two directory groups emit 94.8\% of the observed host links. Directed preferential attachment reaches ROC-AUC 0.976 with random non-edges, but falls to $0.550\pm0.014$ under source-conditioned target-degree matching. With disjoint training and test pairs, multimodal logistic regression reaches $0.672\pm0.021$, GAE $0.899\pm0.016$, and VGAE $0.906\pm0.016$. A four-qubit variational quantum classifier (VQC) comparison tests two encodings across 20 disjoint-pair graph splits under exact and 1,024-shot simulation, with classical controls using the same inputs and training examples. Its best exact mean ROC-AUC is $0.549\pm0.023$, compared with $0.551\pm0.016$ for RBF SVC and $0.573\pm0.029$ for a 16-parameter MLP on the same inputs and training examples. These results support predictive signal in combined graph/content features and show why degree control, feature compression, and optimization conditions matter in quantum--classical comparisons.

title: Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers
authors: Sugam Karki; Raúl Vázquez; Yova Kementchedjhieva
abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.

title: TIE: Training-free CLIP Embedding Guidance for Compositional Text-to-Image Alignment
authors: Sujung Hong; Tae Eun Choi; Youngjun Jun; Chanyong Yoon; Seong Jae Hwang
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have advanced notably, but still fail to satisfy prompt conditions, resulting in attribute mismatches and missing objects. These errors normally fall into two categories: concept loss, when an object or attribute (i.e., concept) goes missing, and concept confusion, when an attribute is assigned to the wrong object or multiple objects blend together. Recent studies suggest that these challenges are caused by the limited capacity of CLIP text encoder to capture fine-grained semantic details. Although several methods have been proposed, concept loss and concept confusion persist in recent T2I models when handling multi-object, multi-attribute prompts. In this paper, we conduct an embedding-level analysis to develop a training-free, inference-time solution for concept loss and concept confusion across CLIP-based T2I models. We find that (1) concepts mentioned later exhibit higher embedding entropy, reflecting less concentrated representations that are more often associated with concept loss, and (2) the first CLIP attention layer captures the strength of binding between each object and its attribute. Guided by our findings, we introduce TIE, a method that improves semantic alignment through a single text-embedding update. TIE addresses concept loss via entropy-aware singular value amplification and resolves concept confusion through interpolation-extrapolation binding based on CLIP attention scores, all in a training-free manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TIE enhances semantic fidelity in multi-concept scenarios with minimal sampling overhead. The project page is available at https://hong-sujung.github.io/TIE/.

title: Organizing Temporal Evidence in Hyperbolic Space for Video Moment Retrieval
authors: Mengnan Liu; Sanping Zhou; Kun Xia; Jiaxuan Lin; Gang Hua; Le Wang
abstract: Video moment retrieval aims to localize a query-relevant temporal segment in an untrimmed video. Existing methods typically perform video-text alignment in Euclidean space, where representations are embedded in a flat geometry. However, accurate moment localization requires organizing query-relevant evidence across multiple grounding states, where target regions, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors exhibit distinct temporal structures and relevance patterns. Such Euclidean representations lack an explicit geometry to jointly capture these relationships, motivating us to explore structured temporal evidence organization from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we propose Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO), a geometric framework that organizes query-aware temporal memory in hyperbolic space. HTEO maps temporal representations into a Poincaré ball and organizes temporal evidence through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR). REO adjusts temporal tokens' radial positions to encode the structural differences among temporal evidence, while OAR enhances query-conditioned semantic alignment through orthogonal rotation. The organized representation is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space and injected into the decoder through a lightweight residual memory update, enabling hyperbolic geometric cues to be incorporated into standard Transformer decoders while preserving the original cross-modal memory. Furthermore, we introduce radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to explicitly guide temporal evidence organization and query-conditioned semantic alignment, respectively. Extensive experiments and analyses across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HTEO improves temporal localization while providing an interpretable geometric organization of temporal evidence.

title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
authors: Radoslaw Malek; Szymon Soltysiak; Aleksandra Kawala-Sterniuk; Piotr Szymanski
abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.

title: Complementing DINO Features with Image Structure for Part Discovery
authors: Samyak Rawlekar; Nikhil Chowdary Paleti; Amey Gupta; Narendra Ahuja
abstract: Self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) like DINO encode rich semantics, enabling training-free segmentation of objects from the background and discovery of their parts via feature clustering. This paper focuses on part discovery: partitioning a foreground object into semantic parts. Existing approaches produce imprecise part boundaries. We trace this to the rigid ViT patch grid used in training DINO, where patches straddling boundaries contain pixels from multiple parts. While DINO's invariance-based training could absorb this pixel-level mixing into clean features, experiments with over 26K foreground patches show it does not: boundary-overlapping patches produce features with higher entropy and lower assignment confidence, blurring predicted part boundaries. Rather than make the massive effort of retraining DINO over geometrically coherent regions, an easier approach is to take boundaries directly from a boundary detector, which supplies the geometric information DINO's features lack. Motivated by this, we introduce Part-DINO, a training-free framework that combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with DINO's semantic features. We use the boundaries to partition the image into regions, pool DINO features within each region, and group them to discover parts. Without any training, Part-DINO produces structurally coherent part assignments, outperforming training-free baselines across four standard benchmarks (CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, PartImageNet-Seg) and remaining competitive with weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods.

title: Representation Learning via Composite Subspace Flow Matching
authors: José Afonso; Mário Figueiredo
abstract: Distilling semantic meaning from raw image data remains a challenge in machine learning. Current self-supervised paradigms face a trade-off: joint-embedding architectures produce relevant features by aggressively discarding intra-class variance, irreversibly spatial and reconstruction. Conversely, generative models preserve spatial details but struggle to isolate semantics, as their optimization is dominated by pixel variations. To bridge this divide, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM). Rather than corrupting data with unstructured isotropic noise, CSFM formulates representation learning as the variance-minimizing inversion of a deterministic degradation curriculum across spectral, color, and illumination subspaces. By bounding trajectory variance with hard temporal style truncation, a capacity-constrained encoder is driven to ignore transient style artifacts and encode persistent content. Empirical evaluations across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 show that CSFM yields competitive discriminative transferability while preserving generative synthesis across both convolutional and vision transformer architectures. By avoiding the collapse pathologies of non-generative methods, CSFM forms a smooth latent space that outperforms standard optimal transport flows on linear probing and few-shot classification, while enabling coherent synthesis and trajectory interpolation. These results confirm that steering the physical dynamics of generative flows offers a scalable paradigm for learning representations that are simultaneously linearly separable and generatively invertible.

title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Hayat; Jahangir Baig; Shayan Ahmed; Ahmed Faraz Ayubi
abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

title: Data Representation at Scale: Extracting Meaningful Knowledge from Massive Datasets
authors: Ylenia Galluzzo
venue: Nova Science Publishers (Nova Science Publishers, Inc.)
abstract: From genomic sequence analysis to real-time sustainability monitoring, and from medical decision support to neurophysiological signal processing, Big Data meaningful knowledge extraction boosts scientific discovery and societal progress. Large-scale biological sequences reveal information about living organisms, while IoT sustainability data show how socio-environmental systems work. Clinical and imaging data support surgery planning, while EEG signals provide insights into cognitive processes. From a computational perspective, these heterogeneous sources share a common issues: transforming raw, high-dimensional, and noisy observations into structured representations that are both machine learning-ready and semantically meaningful.This PhD thesis proposes novel knowledge extraction techniques from heterogeneous and large-scale data, integrating distributed Big Data infrastructures, vector and graph-based representations, and machine learning methods ranging from classical approaches to deep learning. Heterogeneous input data, time series, images, biological sequences, and text, are processed through novel frameworks for meaningful feature extraction and embedding, producing structured latent representations Z ∈ RN×d that support statistical and predictive analysis of learned features in all domains and, in the sustainability domain, a knowledge graph that encodes relational structure between entities.Four application domains are considered: Biological data, Neurophysiological data, Sustainability data, and Medical data. For Biological data, the focus is on analyzing genomic sequences and constructing compact sequence representations that combine two complementary components: a distributed Burrows–Wheeler Transform (BWT) index, providing compressed and searchable access to large sequence collections, and the BioSet2Vec framework, devoted to the extraction of compact and statistically significant k-mer dictionaries that characterize biological sequence sets. With respect to Neurophysiological data, the aim is to extract neural signatures from EEG signals as cognitive knowledge representations. In the Sustainability context, there is modeling of stakeholder relationships via knowledge graphs and real-time energy monitoring via edge–cloud analytics. Lastly, for Medical data multimodal surgical decision support in reductive mastoplasty is addressed via probabilistic fusion of clinical and meaningful morphometric representations.

title: Arabert with Graph Attention for Imbalanced Arabic Sentiment Classification: An Ablation Study of Fusion Strategies
authors: H. A. Ali; A. Sabir
abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether combining AraBERT with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) over a semantic text graph improves three-class classification. Design/Methodology/Approach: Experiments were conducted on hotel reviews (HARD, 392,512 texts) and book reviews (LABR, 59,620 texts). Both corpora are imbalanced in almost identical proportions — negative 13.06%, neutral 19.92%, positive 67.01% in HARD, and 13.13%, 19.47%, 67.40% in LABR. A stratified 70/15/15 split preserves these proportions, giving evaluation partitions of 58,878 and 8,944 reviews, respectively. We compared four configurations: AraBERT alone (M1), a frozen encoder feeding the graph network (M2), a fine-tuned encoder whose sentence representation is replaced by the pooled graph states (M3), and a fine-tuned encoder whose pooled graph states are fused with the retained CLS representation (M4). Each configuration was trained with three seeds on a fixed stratified split. Research Limitation: The paired t-test over three seeds does not reach significance in either corpus. Findings: On LABR, M4 obtained the highest F1-Macro (0.6263 ± 0.0036 against 0.6226 ± 0.0036 for M1), and McNemar's test was significant in two of the three seeds. On HARD, the ordering was reversed (0.8337 ± 0.0040 for M1 against 0.8304 ± 0.0028 for M4). M3 did not exceed the baseline, and M2 fell clearly below it. Practical Implication: Establishing a clearer benefit will require a more precise graph, in particular one derived from syntactic parsing rather than lexical matching, and a tighter form of integration than the concatenation used here. Social Implication: Sentiment analysis is a natural language processing technique which seeks to determine whether the expressed sentiment is positive, negative or neutral so that an institution/researcher can gain insights from a large set of unstructured data. Originality/Value: The study isolates the manner of combination rather than the presence of the graph: fusing the pooled graph states with the retained CLS representation improves on the baseline, whereas substituting them for it does not, a distinction not previously separated for Arabic document-level sentiment.

title: FAMILIAR WORDS, UNFAMILIAR SENSES: A CORPUS-BASED STUDY OF SEMANTIC AMBIGUITY IN THE PUNJAB TEXTBOOK BOARD GRADE 9 ENGLISH TEXTBOOK
authors: Laiba Yousaf; Naveed Nawaz Ahmad; Munazah Ayesha Ameer
abstract: The English textbooks published by the Punjab Textbook Board (PTB) are the main, and often the only, source of English for most students in Punjab's government schools, yet the semantic clarity of their vocabulary has rarely been examined systematically. This study investigates semantic ambiguity in the PTB Grade 9 English textbook through a corpus-based design. The book was digitised as a corpus of approximately 32,500 tokens and explored in AntConc using frequency lists, concordance lines and collocates. Items with ambiguous senses were classified as polysemy, homonymy or vagueness following Cruse (1986) and Lyons (1995), and each was rated for pedagogical risk. Fifty ambiguous items were identified. Polysemy was the most frequent type (52%), followed by vagueness (44%) and homonymy (2%); one further item was a technical term. Ambiguity clustered by genre: poetry and religious texts carried the heaviest polysemous load, civic texts relied on abstract, vague nouns, and informational texts were the least demanding. All 14 items rated high or very high risk were polysemous, and most were familiar words used in extended or figurative senses, such as heart, wealth, sleep and light. None of the glossary entries, marginal notes or exercises addressed any of them, so teachers and learners must disambiguate them unaided. The study recommends marginal glosses, meaning-focused exercises and teacher training in lexical ambiguity. Keywords: semantic ambiguity; polysemy; homonymy; vagueness; corpus linguistics; English textbooks; Punjab Textbook Board; EFL; Pakistan; AntConc

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
authors: Neel Dey; Adrian V. Dalca
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. We use our 3D foundation model, anatomix, to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes and further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific, component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system placed first on the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at https://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
authors: Yang Luo; Tiantian Ji; Zifeng Kang; Yucheng Wang; Yong Liu; Zhiyi Yin; Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).

title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
authors: Zongsheng Li; Shengyuan Zhu; Zimo Zhang; Hanyao Li; Shengming Wang; Quanying Liu
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

title: More Interactions Make Communications More Efficient: A Directed Information Bottleneck Approach to Task-Oriented Communication
authors: Zhirun Zheng; Yiqin Deng; Phone Lin; Yuguang Fang
abstract: Task-oriented communication improves communication efficiency by transmitting semantic information required for downstream tasks, but may incur redundancy with previously transmitted information. To address this issue, we propose a variational directed information bottleneck joint source-channel coding (VDIB-JSCC) framework that transmits only previously unacquired information. Specifically, we use directed information to characterize the causal flow of task-relevant incremental information and theoretically demonstrate its advantages over mutual information and conditional mutual information. Based on this metric, we formulate a directed information bottleneck (DIB) objective that balances task-relevant information preservation and redundant information compression. We further derive a variational formulation, termed VDIB, whose tractable upper bound serves as the training loss. The encoder integrates a Vision Transformer for frame-wise semantic extraction and a Mamba-based causal state-space model for capturing temporal dependencies and extracting incremental information, while the decoder uses a Mamba-based state-space model for task inference. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 video streams demonstrate that VDIB-JSCC achieves higher classification accuracy with less transmitted information than state-of-the-art semantic communication methods. These results show that leveraging historical knowledge enables task completion with less information, improving communication efficiency.

title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
authors: Junming Liu; Marcel Böhme
abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.

title: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset
authors: Mohammad Abolnejadian; Matthew Brehmer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset 📄 Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3830398.3830522💻 Code: https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast Supplemental dataset for the paper: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings Mohammad Abolnejadian and Matthew Brehmer. Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '26). DOI: 10.1145/3830398.3830522 This dataset provides a collection of 43,878 open legislative records from the Canadian House of Commons, spanning 1994 to 2025, covering document types such as debates (Hansard), legislative bills, committee reports, petitions, recorded votes, order papers, and Library of Parliament research publications. It is released at three stages of the same pipeline: the raw collected documents, a processed corpus that has been passed through an ETL pipeline and chunked for use in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, and an embedded, pre-indexed vector store built from that processed corpus. The dataset supports the development and user study of the InsightToast project. The embedded form can be placed directly into the project's codebase, open sourced at https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast, where it serves as the knowledge base when InsightToast operates as a proactive side-channel assistant in policy discussion meetings. Usage in the InsightToast Backend Only qdrant_storage.tar.gz is required to run the backend. Extract it into the root of the InsightToast project, so that qdrant_storage/ sits alongside docker-compose.yml, and start the services: tar -xzf qdrant_storage.tar.gz -C /path/to/InsightToast/ cd /path/to/InsightToast docker compose up --build -d Contents File What it is Approx. size parliament_data.tar.gz Raw source corpus of 43,878 parliamentary records, as 57,124 files (.txt + .pdf) 8.1 GB compressed / 11 GB extracted parliament_data_processed.tar.gz Processed corpus: the same records cleaned, normalized, and chunked into RAG-ready JSON 2.1 GB compressed / 9.1 GB extracted qdrant_storage.tar.gz Pre-indexed Qdrant vector store, ready to mount as the knowledge base 21 GB compressed / 27 GB extracted parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the raw corpus, viewable without downloading the archive small parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the processed corpus small qdrant_storage.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the vector store small SHA256SUMS.txt SHA-256 checksums for the three archives small Verify the archives after download: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt Source Corpus: Raw Parliamentary Documents parliament_data.tar.gz contains open legislative documents collected across the range of record types produced by the Canadian House of Commons and the Library of Parliament, including the proceedings of debate, the texts of bills as tabled, the reports of standing committees, the petitions presented to the House, and the recorded outcomes of divisions. The documents were assembled from three public sources: the House of Commons (ourcommons.ca, including the Legislative Information service, LEGISinfo), the Library of Parliament of Canada (parl-gc.primo.exlibrisgroup.com), and the independent open-data mirror openparliament.ca. No private, personal, or access-restricted material is included; Member of Parliament profiles contain only information published in an official public capacity. Total: 43,878 parliamentary records, distributed across 57,124 files (43,634 .txt + 13,490 .pdf). Each record is provided as extracted plain text, with the source PDF alongside it under the same basename where one exists, so records that carry both formats account for two files. Temporal coverage: documents span the 35th through 45th Parliaments. Debates run from 1994-01-17 to 2025-10-10; coverage of the other record types varies by type. Languages: the source records are bilingual (English and French), as published by Parliament. Filename conventions: debates use sitting dates (YYYY-MM-DD- .txt); bills, journals, order papers, and votes use - - (for example, 37-1-C-10); petitions and Library of Parliament publications use slugified titles. Category Files Description debates/ 18,347 House of Commons debates (Hansard transcripts), one file per sitting day bills/ 10,561 Legislative bills, full text plus the original tabled PDF journals/ 7,038 Official Journals of the House (daily record of decisions) petitions/ 6,093 e-Petitions and paper petitions presented to the House votes/ 4,521 Recorded division and vote results order-papers/ 4,228 Order Paper and Notice Paper (daily agenda) library/ 2,202 Library of Parliament publications and tabled agreements committee-reports/ 1,577 Standing and joint committee reports, grouped into 27 committee subfolders politicians/ 1,319 Member of Parliament profiles research/ 1,210 Library of Parliament research and HillNotes publications committees/ 28 Committee mandate and description summaries Total 57,124 See parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt for the full breakdown, including all committee subfolders. Processed Corpus: Cleaned and Chunked Records parliament_data_processed.tar.gz contains the same corpus after the ETL pipeline that turns each document into retrievable units. Documents are parsed from their metadata header and routed by document_type. Bilingual records are language-identified with langdetect and reduced to their English content by an LLM pass. PDFs are structurally partitioned with unstructured's partition_pdf into text, table, and image elements; table elements are linearized into prose by an LLM, and salient figures are captioned, written to images/, and linked from their chunk via has_images. Records whose content is inherently tabular, namely recorded votes, petitions, and Member profiles, are rendered into natural-language narratives to keep them semantically retrievable rather than reducing to fields. Type-specific pre-segmentation then splits debates on speaker turns, preserving the speaker, section, and timestamp, before every stream passes through a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (1,000 characters, 200 overlap); each resulting chunk is tagged with its content_type (text, table, or image) and its provenance. The output is one JSON document per record, holding the record's metadata and its ordered list of chunks: { "metadata": { "document_type": "debate", "session": "35-1", "date": "1994-01-17", "language": "en", "source_file": "debates/1994-01-17-1.txt", "source_url": "...", "total_chunks": 51 }, "chunks": [ { "chunk_id": 0, "content": "...", "metadata": { "speaker": "...", "section": "...", "content_type": "text", "has_images": false } } ] } Volume: 42,014 JSON records and 2,170 extracted images, totaling 6,379,732 chunks, which is the set embedded into the knowledge base below. Traceability: every record's metadata.source_file links back to its file in the raw corpus. Coverage: most record types are processed in full; committee-report and library are present as subsets of the raw corpus. See parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt for per-category counts. Indexed Knowledge Base qdrant_storage.tar.gz contains the processed corpus above embedded and indexed into Qdrant, ready to serve as the retrieval backend with no further processing. title: The Impact of Business Environmental Changes on the Adoption of a Strategic Pivot: A Case Study of Zar Industrial Group
authors: Alireza Mansourkhaki; Kambiz Talebi; Jahangir Yadollahi Farsi
venue: International Journal of Innovation Management and Organizational Behavior (IJIMOB)
abstract: Objective: This study aimed to examine the impact of business environmental changes on strategic pivot adoption in Zar Industrial Group and develop a conceptual model of this process. Methods and Materials: This applied qualitative study used a grounded theory design. The study population consisted of Zar Industrial Group managers and university professors with expertise in strategic management and organizational change. Participants were selected purposively based on their knowledge and professional experience. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with managers of the holding company and its food-industry subsidiaries, together with academic experts. Interviews continued until theoretical saturation, resulting in a final sample of 12 participants. Interview transcripts were systematically coded, compared, and categorized to identify the principal dimensions and mechanisms associated with strategic pivot adoption. Findings: The analysis produced seven main categories and 41 related concepts. The categories included macro-environmental changes and external pressures; risk, uncertainty, and financial pressure; supply-chain and operational disruptions; market-oriented and commercial responses; structural and business-model redesign; innovation, technology, and digital transformation; and human capital, organizational learning, and institutionalization of the strategic pivot. Environmental turbulence generated financial, operational, and market pressures that stimulated coordinated strategic responses. These responses involved market reorientation, business-model redesign, technological innovation, digital transformation, and capability development. Human capital and organizational learning played a central role in sustaining and institutionalizing the strategic pivot. Conclusion: Strategic pivot adoption in Zar Industrial Group represents a multidimensional organizational response to environmental uncertainty rather than an isolated managerial decision. Successful pivots require alignment among market responses, structural transformation, technological innovation, operational resilience, and organizational learning. The proposed conceptual model can help managers recognize environmental signals, coordinate adaptive actions, and strengthen organizational resilience and long-term competitiveness.

title: Deep Learning-Based Object Detection for Fashion, Uniform, and PPE Items: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Isa Aulia Almadani; Nurcahya Pradana Taufik Prakisya; Cucuk Wawan Budiyanto
venue: Journal of Information Systems and Informatics
abstract: Deep learning-based object detection for clothing and uniform items spans two research streams: fashion and apparel detection for e-commerce, and personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance detection for occupational safety. No prior review has jointly synthesized these streams with a detection-centric scope. This study addresses that gap through a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic literature review of 1,378 records from Scopus as the sole database, identified via two Boolean queries and screened for object detection or instance segmentation of clothing, uniform, or PPE items, yielding 26 empirical studies published between 2021 and 2026. One-stage YOLO-based detectors dominate the corpus (18 of 26 studies, up to 96.9% mAP50 at 7.3 ms inference), a dominance partly attributable to an architectural constraint in the PPE-domain search query; two-stage R-CNN and transformer-based architectures remain comparatively underexplored, the latter represented by only two studies. Dataset scale is markedly asymmetric between public fashion benchmarks (up to 491,895 images) and PPE-specific collections (as few as 1,330 images), though an emerging benchmark-reuse pattern partly offsets this gap within the PPE domain. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis benchmarked against five prior reviews, an explicit architecture-dataset-metric mapping, a proposed nine-element minimum reporting standard, and a challenge taxonomy that surfaces previously undiscussed ethical and cultural-representation gaps in this literature
